summary: This bill prohibits the FCC from requiring any regulated entity to align its speech or editorial content with the political ideology of any presidential administration, including through rules, orders, or conditions on mergers and approvals.

scores.thoughts: The bill contains no provisions related to federal spending, appropriations, or budget authority. It solely addresses FCC regulatory powers over speech alignment.
No tax provisions, rate changes, credits, or revenue measures appear in the bill text.
The legislation does not address healthcare policy, insurance, providers, or coverage models.
No references to firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
The bill makes no mention of immigration, border policy, visas, or related enforcement.
No content concerning reproductive rights, abortion access, or restrictions.
No provisions affecting military budgets, defense policy, or armed forces.
The bill does not engage with environmental regulations, climate policy, or energy standards.
No welfare, entitlement, or social assistance programs are addressed.
The legislation contains nothing related to schools, education funding, or curriculum policy.
No references to controlled substances, decriminalization, or drug enforcement.
The bill does not touch sentencing, policing, incarceration, or criminal procedure.
No trade agreements, tariffs, or import/export regulations are involved.
The bill has no fiscal impact language or debt-related provisions.
While the bill protects entities from compelled speech alignment, it does not specifically address LGBTQ+ legal protections or rights.
No foreign assistance, international aid, or State Department funding provisions.
The legislation does not address voting access, election administration, or campaign rules.
The bill limits FCC authority over content/speech policies for regulated entities but does not address data privacy, surveillance, or tech platform regulation in the sense of the topic definition.
No labor, union, or workplace rights provisions are present.
The bill protects editorial independence from government ideological mandates but does not directly prioritize religious exemptions versus anti-discrimination rules.
